Future dollars and today’s purchasing power need matching discount rates

Four charts price the same future spending plan in nominal and real terms, verify equal present costs, and expose the errors from mixing the two bases.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 6 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Match the cash-flow price basis to the discount-rate price basis

Interactive planning lab

Present cost omitted by mixing real cash with the nominal rate$42,341.49

Original deterministic annual-cost illustration. The entered cost has constant starting-date purchasing power. The first payment is at the END of year one, so its nominal amount already includes one year of the selected price growth; the final payment is at the selected year-end. All rates are effective annual. “Nominal” here means a money/price basis that includes the assumed inflation effect, not a nominal compounding-frequency quote. Equivalent real discount growth equals nominal discount growth divided by price growth; the real rate can be negative and is not clamped to zero. Correct nominal-cash/nominal-rate and real-cash/real-rate valuations describe the same payment plan at time zero. Two deliberately mismatched calculations illustrate basis errors, not alternative legitimate cost forecasts. No account balance, saving contribution, portfolio return, tax, fee, household risk model or funding adequacy is calculated. Constant inflation and discount assumptions are independently entered scenarios, not official forecasts or recommended personal rates. Full-precision rates are used in calculations even when the displayed real rate is rounded.

The central idea

Either consistent route works: discount inflation-indexed nominal payments at the matching nominal rate, or constant-real payments at the equivalent real rate. Keep the payment dates and full-precision conversion the same.

01

Name the price basis before entering the amount

A future spending estimate can be stated in the dollars expected to be paid on its date or in the purchasing power of a common starting date. Both descriptions can be useful, but the label must travel with the number.

The original plan requires the purchasing-power equivalent of CAD 12,000 at each of twenty year-ends. It assumes a constant 3% annual increase in the price level. The real amount stays CAD 12,000 in starting-date purchasing-power dollars, while the nominal payment grows with the assumed price level.

The first payment occurs at the end of year one, after one complete year of price growth. Its nominal amount is CAD 12,360. The twentieth payment is approximately CAD 21,673.33 in payment-date dollars. These are two nominal amounts buying the same modeled annual quantity under the chosen inflation assumption.

The first chart places the nominal and constant-real descriptions beside each other. They are not two separate bills, and their vertical gap is not an increase in real consumption. The plan is deliberately constant in purchasing power; no age-related spending change, personal inflation basket or actual future price quote is inferred.

02

Convert annual growth factors, rather than rounding a subtraction

The nominal discount assumption is 6% effective annually. Here “nominal” identifies the price basis of the rate, including the assumed inflation effect. It does not mean a nominal annual interest quote with a separate compounding frequency.

The matching effective annual real discount assumption is (1.06 ÷ 1.03) − 1, approximately 2.912621%. The tool keeps that full-precision value even though the metric displays a rounded percentage.

More generally, 1 + nominal rate = (1 + real rate) × (1 + inflation). ACCA’s investment-appraisal explanation describes this growth-factor relationship and the matching of real cash flows to real rates and nominal cash flows to nominal rates.

Simply subtracting 3% from 6% gives an approximation of 3%, not the exact equivalent rate in this model. Reusing a rounded displayed real rate can also introduce a difference between routes. The conversion changes the unit basis consistently; it does not identify an investment that will deliver either assumed rate.

03

Verify the same present cost in both consistent routes

For the first payment, the nominal route discounts CAD 12,360 by 1.06, producing about CAD 11,660.38 at time zero. The real route discounts CAD 12,000 by 1.06 ÷ 1.03 and produces the same present cost.

For a payment at year t, the nominal route is 12,000 × 1.03t ÷ 1.06t. Rearranging gives 12,000 ÷ (1.06 ÷ 1.03)t, exactly the real route. The equality holds payment by payment, not just after a coincidental cancellation in the final sum.

Adding all twenty correctly discounted year-end payments gives approximately CAD 179,980.54 in starting-date present-cost dollars. The second chart shows the two matched totals together. The annual-contribution chart draws one correct line because the other consistent calculation would obscure it by lying on top of it.

Present cost is a valuation, not a current bank balance or an amount guaranteed to fund the plan under market uncertainty. The model supplies no investment account, saving schedule, tax cash or retirement-adequacy assessment. Its purpose is to ensure that changing the description of the same plan does not change the arithmetic value.

04

Inspect what happens when the price bases are mixed

The third row of the total comparison takes the constant-real CAD 12,000 payments and discounts them at the 6% nominal rate. That mismatched calculation gives about CAD 137,639.05, understating the matched present cost by about CAD 42,341.49.

The fourth row makes the opposite mismatch: it grows payments with inflation and then discounts those nominal payments at the smaller equivalent real rate. Its result is approximately CAD 242,151.17. The same plan now appears more expensive because the price-basis adjustment has been handled inconsistently.

These rows are intentionally incorrect calculations of the stated plan. They are not alternative genuine price forecasts, recommended discount methods or competing investment outcomes. Their labels retain the mismatch so that the difference cannot be mistaken for extra risk protection or better returns.

The annual present-cost chart locates the distortion across payment dates. Each point is one future payment’s contribution to time-zero value. Later payments can be affected more because the inconsistent price-basis factors compound for more years.

05

Zero inflation and negative real rates help check the model

Set inflation to zero and the two price bases coincide. The equivalent real rate equals the nominal rate, the nominal payments stay at the constant-real amount, and both deliberate price-basis mismatches disappear.

If the nominal discount assumption equals inflation, the equivalent real rate is zero. Each constant-real payment then contributes its full entered amount to present cost. With twenty CAD 12,000 payments, that consistent total is CAD 240,000.

If the nominal assumption is below inflation, the equivalent real rate is negative. The tool retains that result. Clamping it to zero would change the stated relationship and break the equality of the consistent routes. A negative real discount assumption does not mean the nominal bill is negative or that a portfolio account has been simulated.

The matrix varies assumed inflation by row and nominal discount assumptions by column, retaining the entered cost and payment count. Cells show the percentage error from the real-cash/nominal-rate mismatch relative to the correctly matched result. A zero-cost plan has no defined percentage error, so its cells remain N/A rather than becoming invented zero observations.

06

Keep the same timing, currency and scope when updating a plan

HM Treasury’s Green Book distinguishes discounting from inflation adjustment and requires its real appraisal rate to be paired with real values. That is useful consistency context; its public-sector social discount rates are not adopted as household rates in this guide.

For a household model, record whether each bill is in starting-date or payment-date money, which price-growth assumption converts it, when payment occurs and which effective annual discount assumption applies. Keep taxes and costs consistent with the chosen scope as well.

Changing a payment from a year-end to a year-start is a timing change, not a price-basis conversion. Changing inflation without updating the corresponding real rate also changes the assumptions. Comparing outputs is useful only after those differences have been identified.

The plan here uses one constant price-growth assumption for all payments. Specific expenses may move differently from general inflation, and uncertain future cash flows need more than a deterministic identity. Use supported inputs and appropriate scenarios for those questions. Matching the bases first keeps those later judgments from being mixed with an avoidable calculation error.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. All spending, inflation and discount assumptions are original hypothetical scenarios. The figures illustrate a deterministic price-basis identity and deliberate mismatches. No official inflation forecast, recommended household discount rate, portfolio outcome or funding adequacy is asserted. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. ACCA · Inflation and investment appraisal ↗

    Reviewed 25 October 2026 for the Fisher growth-factor relationship and consistent real/nominal discounting. No publisher project example, tax calculation, table or rate assumption is reproduced.

  2. HM Treasury · The Green Book 2026, discounting ↗

    Updated 5 February 2026; reviewed 25 October 2026. Supports the distinction between inflation adjustment and discounting and the matching of real values with a real appraisal rate. The guide does not adopt UK social discount rates or public-sector appraisal rules as personal recommendations.

  3. Aswath Damodaran, NYU Stern · A primer on the time value of money ↗

    Reviewed 25 October 2026 for dated cash flows, common-date valuation and discounting context. No historical return estimate, figure or worked example is reproduced.
